newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb official rules out dinar devaluation - Tanjug.
newsitem.headline: Serb official rules out dinar devaluation - Tanjug.

text.p: A senior Serbian government official ruled out a devaluation of the dinar, warning local businesses who were counting on it that they were taking a big risk.
"There will be no devaluation and if someone's waiting for it, he is entering a major business risk," Deputy Prime Minister Jovan Radulovic said in an interview with Tanjug news agency on Sunday.

The minister said economic growth targets, while ambitious, were not unrealistic and the government expected they would be met, though he added that difficulties in Yugoslavia's reintegration into world markets were greater than expected.
"Production trends are now good, although manufacturers were not immediately prepared to begin because of the lack of raw and production materials," he said.
International trade sanctions imposed on rump Yugoslavia for its part in the Bosnia war were lifted only last November.

He said Yugoslav's business reputation had not disappeared in the past past four years, but foreign investments could not be expected unless relations with the International Monetary Fund were regulated and other formal preconditions met.
The chief prerequisite for the inflow of foreign capital was the lifting of the "outer wall" of sanctions barring Yugoslavia from international financial institutions, he added.
"World bankers are trying to find out what our stand on privatization is and what legal security we guarantee for investments," he said.
He said interest in investing here was growing as the positive elements of the Yugoslav economic and political system were clear from measures the government was taking.

The minister said the Serbian government's privatization bill was almost drafted and would be discussed in 10 days. Without privatization, the Yugoslav economy would be excluded from European markets, he stressed.
Radulovic said the Serbian government was dissatisfied with the current degree of foreign trade liberalization, and called for freer imports and exports.
